common_name: Hope Springs Eternal Hosta (Shadowland Series Ruffled Blue Hosta)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring or early fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, giving this large selection room to reach its mature spread.

directions: Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, away from hot afternoon sun that can scorch the heavily ruffled leaf margins. Named the 2026 Hosta of the Year, this Shadowland-series selection forms a dense clump of heart-shaped, blue-green leaves edged in a crisp, creamy white band, with dramatic rippling that runs from the leaf base all the way to the tip. Near-white, lightly fragrant flowers rise on scapes well above the foliage in midsummer, drawing pollinators and adding vertical interest to what is otherwise a low, mounding specimen. Its strong growth rate and heavy substance make it a good candidate for a shaded focal point or large container where the ruffled edge can be appreciated up close.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, allowing the creeping rhizomes room to spread into a slow groundcover patch.

directions: Site in humus-rich, well-drained soil that stays evenly moist through the growing season, in partial to full woodland shade. This diminutive Chinese relative of Solomon's seal stays low to the ground on wiry, wandering rhizomes, sending up glossy evergreen foliage that persists through mild winters and slowly knits together into a fine-textured groundcover. Small, bell-shaped white flowers dangle beneath the arching stems in spring, followed by inconspicuous berries. Because it colonizes gradually rather than aggressively, it suits the front of a shaded border or a woodland path edge where a low, undemanding evergreen carpet is wanted beneath taller ferns and hostas.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in dappled to full shade; this species is less cold-hardy than Disporopsis pernyi, so give it a sheltered site at the northern edge of its range.

directions: Grow in moist but well-drained, organically rich soil in dappled or full shade, mimicking the plant's native Chinese forest-floor understory. Creeping rhizomes send up gracefully arching stems clothed in glossy, pale to mid-green oval leaves that remain evergreen where winters stay mild. Small, whitish, faintly speckled bell-shaped flowers dangle from the leaf axils in late spring, followed by dark berries later in the season. Best used as a fine-textured, clump-forming accent tucked among rocks or at the base of shrubs in a shaded border, where its low arching habit contrasts nicely with bolder-leaved shade perennials.

planting.note: Plant rooted plantlets or divisions in spring in humus-rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; in cold climates it is often grown as a container or hanging-basket plant and overwintered indoors.

directions: Grow in evenly moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, sheltered from hot direct sun that can bleach the variegation. This selection carries the same rounded, olive-green leaves with silvery veining and red-purple undersides as the species, but each leaf is irregularly edged in creamy white, and in brighter light the new growth and margins often take on a soft pink blush. Slender red runners trail outward and root at the tip to form new plantlets, quickly building a spreading mat, while airy sprays of small white, asymmetrical flowers appear on thin stems in late spring. It excels tumbling over the edge of a shaded raised bed, rock wall, or hanging basket where the trailing runners can be shown off.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or fall in humus-rich, consistently moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, protecting the emerging fall flower stalks from early hard frosts.

directions: Site in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, out of drying wind and hot midday sun. An Award of Garden Merit selection valued for its low mound of glossy, rounded leaves in a rich bronzy-red that deepens through the season, contrasting sharply with sprays of small, star-shaped white flowers that appear on wiry red stems in late summer into fall, later than almost any other woodland perennial. It is a collector-favorite accent for the front of a shaded border or beside stepping stones, where the dark foliage color can be appreciated at close range against paler companions such as ferns or heucheras.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or fall in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, where the clump can be left undisturbed to build size over several seasons.

directions: Grow in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, sheltered from strong afternoon sun. This named selection forms a clump of glossy, lobed leaves with coppery overtones on top and a rich red flush beneath, larger and more vigorous than many other fortunei cultivars. Tall, wiry red stems carry dense, airy clouds of small white flowers held well above the foliage in autumn, at a time when few other shade perennials are still in bloom. It works well massed at the edge of a woodland path or beneath deciduous shrubs, where the late flower display and colorful foliage extend seasonal interest into the fall garden.

common_name: Black Ruby Fall Saxifrage (Dark-Leaved Woodland Saxifrage)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or fall in humus-rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, siting the clump where the dark foliage can be viewed against lighter companions.

directions: Plant in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, avoiding hot afternoon sun that fades the foliage color. Grown chiefly for its near-black, deeply lobed purple foliage, this Japanese selection holds its dark coloring from spring through fall, making it a striking foliage accent well before its late display of airy, star-shaped pink flowers held above the leaves from September into November. Because the color is most intense with cooler root conditions, mulch to keep the shallow root run from drying out through summer heat. It is best used in small groupings at the front of a shaded border, in a trough, or alongside pale-leaved hostas and ferns where the contrast in foliage tone can be fully appreciated.

common_name: Golden London Pride (Variegated London Pride Saxifrage)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; this variegated selection is slower and less vigorous than plain London Pride and benefits from removing any all-green reverted rosettes.

directions: Grow in evenly moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, an undemanding groundcover for poor or rooty ground where little else will thrive. Low evergreen rosettes of scalloped, spoon-shaped leaves are irregularly splashed and speckled with gold, brightening shaded ground year-round even without flowers. In late spring, haze-like sprays of small, star-shaped white flowers flushed pink rise on thin, wiry stems well above the foliage mat. Use it as an edging plant along a shaded path or at the front of a woodland border, where the gold-flecked foliage catches the eye long after the brief spring bloom has passed.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, allowing generous room for the outsized foliage to spread.

directions: Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, keeping the root zone from ever drying out since the enormous leaves wilt quickly under water stress. This selected clone of giant leopard plant produces rounded, kidney-shaped leaves that can approach fifteen inches across, thick and glossy enough to look almost artificial, dwarfing the standard species and most other Farfugium cultivars. Clusters of daisy-like yellow flowers rise above the bold foliage clump in fall. Best reserved for a large-scale shaded planting, pondside bed, or big container where its outsized, tropical-looking leaves can serve as a dramatic focal point rather than competing for space with smaller companions.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, siting it as a specimen accent rather than a mass planting given its unusual, sought-after form.

directions: Grow in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, keeping soil moisture consistent through the growing season. This oddity among leopard plant cultivars produces thick, crinkled, swollen leaves that curl and contort into bizarre, sculptural shapes rather than the typical flat rounded leaf of the species, making it a reliable conversation piece in the shade garden. In October, flower spikes rise roughly two feet above the foliage clump, topped with the same bright yellow daisy-like blooms typical of the genus. Because of its slow growth and collector appeal, it is best featured singly in a container or as a specimen accent near a shaded entry or patio rather than combined into a mixed bed.
